text: - That the carriage of oxygen should be mandatory for persons operating commercial snorkelling tours.
- That the carriage of an Automated External Defibrillator should be mandatory for persons operating commercial snorkelling tours.
- That SafeWork SA conduct an audit of snorkelling tours in South Australia and report to the Coroners Court on its findings.

- That SafeWork SA advise the Coroner of the extent to which operators within South Australia are compliant with the SafeWork SA Snorkel Safety Guidelines and whether SafeWork SA are of the view that the current legislation allows them to enforce any incidence of non-compliance.

- That persons operating commercial snorkelling tours consider the purchase and placement of defibrillators within their workplaces where patrons are undertaking snorkelling activities. Response from the South Australian Government - Commentary •   The first five recommendations were directed to the Minister for Recreation, Sport and Racing. These recommendations relate to making it mandatory for persons operating commercial snorkelling tours to carry oxygen and automated external defibrillators, and for operators to consider making defibrillators within their workplace publicly available to its patrons. •   The Minister for Recreation, Sport and Racing notes that although the Minister is responsible for active recreational activities, including recreational snorkelling, the powers referred to by the Coroner sit within the remit of the Minister for Industrial Relations and Public Sector and are exercised through SafeWork SA. •   Recommendations 3 and 4 were directed to SafeWork SA, which sits under the Minister for Industrial Relations and Public Sector. These two recommendations relate to SafeWork SA’s activities about monitoring and enforcing compliance under work health and safety legislation. •   The recommendations directed to the Attorney-General (6 and 7) relate to introducing regulatory requirements for all businesses conducting snorkelling activities to carry emergency oxygen units as part of their first aid duties, their staff must be trained and available to administer oxygen, and that they must include automated external defibrillators as part of their emergency response equipment. •   The Ministers have consulted with the following agencies about the Coroner’s recommendations and their comments have been included in the Report where relevant: a)   The Australian Maritime and Safety Authority (AMSA), responsible as the regulator for vessels outside the 3 nautical mile limit b)   The Department of Environment and Water (DEW), responsible for licensing commercial activities, including commercial tours offering recreational snorkelling, in National Parks and Marine Parks 17 | P a g e OFFICIAL OFFICIAL

- That legislation be introduced requiring all businesses conducting snorkelling activities to carry an emergency oxygen unit as part of their first aid supplies and that operators ensure that there is always a member of staff available who is appropriately trained to administer oxygen.

- That legislation be introduced requiring all businesses conducting snorkelling activities to carry an Automated External Defibrillator. Response from the South Australian Government with respect to Recommendations 6 and 7 •   To achieve this, SafeWork SA will commence the process to introduce amendments to South Australia’s approved First Aid in the Workplace Code of Practice June 2020 (Code), which serves as an enforceable legislative instrument under the Work Health and Safety Act 2012 (SA). •   The Code is based on a national model code of practice developed by Safe Work Australia under the national harmonisation of work health and safety legislation and has been approved under section 274 of the Work Health and Safety Act 2012 (SA). •   The Minister for Industrial Relations and Public Sector will progress the proposed amendments to the SafeWork SA Advisory Committee (advisory committee), established under Division 5 of the Work Health and Safety Act 2012 (SA) from 1 September 2024, for consideration of if the Code should be amended. The Minister may only approve, vary or revoke a code of practice if the Minister is acting on the recommendation of the advisory committee and that code of practice, variation or revocation was developed by a process that involved consultation between the Governments of the Commonwealth and each State and Territory, unions and employer organisations. The changes to South Australia’s Code will require businesses conducting diving and snorkelling activities to: a)   carry automated external defibrillators and emergency oxygen units as part of their first aid and emergency response equipment, and 19 | P a g e OFFICIAL OFFICIAL 2024-25 ANNUAL REPORT for the Coroners Court b)   ensure that there is always at least one member of staff available at the immediate workplace who is appropriately trained to administer the oxygen supply. Consultation with other agencies

- That education and information on the diagnosis of infective endocarditis, particularly its prevalence with known illicit intravenous drug users, be disseminated throughout the Local Health Networks of South Australia. Response from SA Health •   The recommendation has been accepted. All Local Health Networks, SA Ambulance Service and Commission on Excellence and Innovation in Health have presented the findings from this inquest at relevant meetings to embed learnings into practice. •   All Local Health Networks and SA Ambulance Service are updating clinical information, and training programs to expand on the importance of IV drug use as a significant risk factor for infective endocarditis.

- That consideration be given by all parties to an in-principle review and/or review of information sharing protocols and systems between hospitals and the SA Ambulance Service in order to provide the most complete history for medical officers dealing with patients who have had involvement with ambulance services out of hospital, relevant to the presentation in hospital. Response from SA Health •   The recommendation is accepted.          SA Health acknowledges the importance of clinical handover and information sharing between services, all Local Health Networks and SA Ambulance Service are committed to continuous monitoring and improvement of effective communication and access to patient information. •   SA Ambulance Service are working towards the implementation of an electronic patient care record (ePCR) as a mechanism for information sharing across the health system. The procurement process is in progress with a plan developed to implement this system in 2025/26. A requirement of the ePCR is connectivity and integration of SA Ambulance Service records with the DHW electronic medical record (Sunrise EMR) so that clinicians can view SAAS patient history. Evans, Caleb (a pseudonym – name suppressed) (Coroner Whittle)

- To the Minister for Child Protection and the Minister for Health and Wellbeing, I recommend that the CYPSA be amended to require a court which finds a parent of a child guilty of an offence against Section 14A of the CLCA to notify both DCP and CaFHS. 20 | P a g e OFFICIAL OFFICIAL 2024-25 ANNUAL REPORT for the Coroners Court Response from the South Australian Government •   This recommendation is accepted in principle. Noting the strength of existing reporting pathways, agencies support the development of a reporting pathway from the CAA to DCP and CaFHS upon a conviction being recorded pursuant to section 14A of the CLC Act within a policy framework.

- To the Minister for Child Protection, I recommend that that the CYPSA be amended to require the Minister or the Chief Executive (of the DCP) to apply to the Youth Court for an order that a parenting capacity assessment be undertaken when a parent who still has a child or children in their care has been found guilty of an offence against Section 14A of the CLCA. Response from the South Australian Government •   This recommendation is accepted in principle. DCP agrees with the importance of undertaking timely and responsive parenting capacity assessments to best inform case direction at relevant points of decision making. DCP has a strong history of utilising existing provisions to seek a parenting capacity assessment when required under section 36(2) of the Children and Young People (Safety) Act 2017. •   DCP supports an amendment to policy to require DCP staff to refer for a parenting capacity assessment where a parent has a child in their care and has been found guilty of an offence under section 14A of the Criminal Law Consolidation Act 1935.

- To the Minister for Child Protection and the Minister for Health and Wellbeing, I recommend that a policy or protocol be developed providing for CaFHS to notify DCP when a parent with a known child protection history opts out of CaFHS involvement with a new infant. Response from the South Australian Government •   This recommendation is accepted. Agencies acknowledge the importance of timely and open information sharing and support the review of existing policies or protocols that detail the reporting obligations of CaFHS and SA Health staff to DCP in matters where a relevant parent disengages from a CaFHS service.

- To the Minister for Child Protection and the Minister for Health and Wellbeing, I recommend that a policy or protocol be developed providing for Unborn Child Concern notifications to be shared by DCP with CaFHS. Response from the South Australian Government •   This recommendation is accepted. Agencies support the continuous improvement of practice, noting there has been positive progress within both agencies to strengthen assessment and responses to Unborn Child Concerns (‘UCC’). This activity includes (but is not limited to): •    Development of an evidenced informed and culturally responsive UCC and High Risk Infant (HRI) Model of Care for DCP. •    Engagement with the Australian Centre for Child Protection to develop an interagency protocol for vulnerable infants. •    Establishment of a DCP HRI Worker Community of Practice to support continuous professional development, best practice approaches and consistency. •    Participation in the SA Health Improvement Project - High Risk Infant Removals at SA Health Sites. •    Development of a contemporary, multidisciplinary workforce model for UCCs and HRIs. •   Specific to this recommendation, agencies support the development of a data sharing agreement between DCP and CaFHS, which will be progressed as part of the development of the DCP UCC/High Risk Infant Model of Care. 21 | P a g e OFFICIAL OFFICIAL 2024-25 ANNUAL REPORT for the Coroners Court

- To the Minister for Child Protection and the Chief Executive of the Department for Child Protection, I recommend: 1)   That the phasing out of the closure of intakes and files due to lack of resources, as recommended in

of The Life They Deserve, be completed within 18 months of the date of this finding; and 2)   That after nine months from the date of this finding, no intake be closed due to lack of resources without the specific approval in writing of the Chief Executive of the Department for Child Protection. Response from the South Australian Government •    This recommendation is accepted in principle. The Government of South Australia accepted recommendation 62 of ‘The Life They Deserve’ in principle on the basis that it would implement system changes that would likely result in many children and families who did not receive a response or service now being assessed and supported. However, the response noted that case allocation is demand driven. •    The number of screened-in notifications increased by 83% over the three financial years following release of the Nyland report – a rate of growth not anticipated at the time the Nyland report was released. •    Despite this growth in notifications, through the significant efforts and reform settings of the State Government, significant inroads are being made in increasing the capacity of the system to respond to the growing number of notifications received. From 2017-18 to 2022-23, the number of notifications investigated or referred increased by 188%, while cases that do not proceed steadily decreased from 55.5% in 2017-18 to 18.1% for 2023-24. In fact, South Australia are now national leaders in completing investigations within the nationally agreed timeframes from receipt of the notification. •    The State Government has allocated significant funding to enhance the child protection and family support system, investing in Intensive Family Services and Family Group Conferencing as meaningful pathways to address growing demand on the sector. •    DCP is reframing the system towards a public health approach, in which all agencies have a role to play in upholding the safety and wellbeing of children and young people across the State. •    Since the Nyland report, systemic changes have been introduced which improve the capacity of the State to offer a more targeted response to screened in notifications. •    The Children and Young People (Safety and Support) Bill 2024 currently before Parliament seeks to embed this public health approach, to better meet community expectations as to when a targeted or a range of other interventions are required to address risk, and when a wider whole of government and community response

- To the Minister for Child Protection and the Chief Executive of the Department for Child Protection, I recommend that (if Recommendation 40 of ‘The Life They Deserve’ is not to be implemented) a policy 22 | P a g e OFFICIAL OFFICIAL 2024-25 ANNUAL REPORT for the Coroners Court be developed which identifies the circumstances in which a notifier is to be advised, or not advised, that a notification has been closed with no action. Response from the South Australian Government •   This recommendation is not accepted. DCP has given effect to recommendation 40 of ‘The Life They Deserve’ by ensuring that notifiers who make a report through the eCARL reporting system are provided with confirmation that their notification has been received. •   Adopting a practice to inform notifiers that a report has been closed with no action could have unintended consequences, such as compromising an SA Police investigation or dissuading a notifier from making future notifications which could compromise the safety of a child or young person. Fisher, Lynne Patricia (Coroner Kereru)

- That the Royal Australian College of General Practitioners release an alert to its members educating them on, and explaining the importance of, the risk scores and ‘red flags’ relating to community acquired pneumonia. Response from RACGP •   The RACGP SA has released this alert as part of the September 2024 newsletter to members. The article (below) reminds members of the importance of risk stratifying patients with community acquired pneumonia and drawing their attention to SA Health pathways, clinical guideline and Antibiotic red flags. Members have been reminded of the above via our Council and regular Faculty communication channels. Community Acquired Pneumonia – Coroner’s report Following a coroner’s case in SA related to a patient who sadly died from Community Acquired Pneumonia (CAP), the SA Coroner has requested that we remind members of the importance of risk stratifying patients with CAP. Accurate assessment of a patient’s risk of an adverse outcome is key to ensuring the most appropriate location for treatment and type of therapy that can be determined. There is an SA Health Pathway for CAP which can be accessed from SA Health Pathways. The guideline includes information for assessment, investigation and management of mild and moderate CAP, and indications for admission. The Australian Therapeutics Guidelines: Antibiotic ‘red flags’ is another useful resource. Comorbidities and social circumstances should also be considered when deciding on patient admission to hospital. For more information, refer to the SA Health Clinical Guideline on Community Acquired Pneumonia.

- That SA Health release an alert to all South Australian Licensed Private Hospitals that treat patients in an emergency setting educating them on, and explaining the importance of, the risk score and ‘red flags’ relating to community acquired pneumonia. Response from SA Health •   The recommendation has been accepted. An alert was released providing advice to hospitals and health care providers (including private hospitals) about the risks and responses to community acquired pneumonia and sepsis as part of World Sepsis Day on 13 September 2024, through the public health information alert system. The alert promoted the Communicable Disease Communication Branch (CDCB) Community Acquired Pneumonia pathway, guidance, and website information. 23 | P a g e OFFICIAL OFFICIAL 2024-25 ANNUAL REPORT for the Coroners Court Response to Recommendations - Deaths In Custody During the year the subject of this report, the following reports detailing any actions taken or proposed to be taken in consequence of recommendations made in the case of a death in custody, were received by the State Coroner: Lens, Christopher (Coroner White) Recommendation - I support the recommendation of the investigating officer in this matter and recommend that a complete review of all detention orders be undertaken by SACAT and other relevant bodies to ensure compliance with relevant acts for the protection and care of vulnerable persons subject to an order. Response from SACAT •   When a SACAT member creates an order in SACAT’s online case management system, it is a mandatory field requirement for the member to select the review date from the list of review periods. While the system prevents the absence of a review date, there is scope for human error if the member incorrectly chooses the period for review.
